ECE 6390

Dish feed: spillover and edge taper

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows a broad and a narrow feed at the focus of an F/D = 0.4 paraboloid: the broad feed spills power past the rim while the narrow feed leaves the dish edge dim.

A parabolic reflector turns the spherical wave from a feed at its focus into an equal-phase plane across its mouth. Seen from the focus, the rim lies at the angle ψ₀ given by tan(ψ₀/2) = D/(4F), where F is the focal length and D the diameter. Feed radiation inside ψ₀ lands on the dish and becomes aperture illumination; radiation beyond ψ₀ misses the reflector and is lost as spillover.

Model the feed power pattern as cos^q ψ toward the dish, where a larger q means a narrower feed. Weighting by the solid-angle factor sin ψ gives the spilled fraction P_spill/P_feed = cos^(q+1) ψ₀. The aperture field reached at feed angle ψ is proportional to √(cos^q ψ)·(1 + cos ψ)/2; the second factor is the extra spreading over the longer path to the rim.

A uniformly lit aperture gives the most gain for its area. The taper efficiency η_t = 2(∫E r dr)²/∫E² r dr, with r the normalized aperture radius, measures how far a tapered field falls short of that. Spillover efficiency η_s = 1 − cos^(q+1) ψ₀ and taper efficiency multiply. A broad feed keeps η_t high but spills; a narrow feed spills little but wastes the edge. Their product peaks with the edge roughly 10 dB below the centre.

Blockage by the feed and its supports, surface and phase errors, and cross-polarization lower efficiency further. Together they explain why practical dishes reach overall aperture efficiencies near 0.55–0.70, such as the η_a = 0.60 used in the link examples.

Example

At F/D = 0.4 the rim is at ψ₀ = 64.0°. A q = 1 feed spills 19.2 % with the edge at −6.4 dB, for an aperture efficiency of 77 %. A q = 4 feed spills only 1.6 % but tapers the edge to −17.2 dB, giving 76 %. The q = 2 feed between them puts the edge at −10 dB and reaches about 83 %.

Practice

1. With the same feed pattern, what happens to the rim angle and the spillover when F/D increases from 0.4 to 0.8?

Use tan(ψ₀/2) = D/(4F) and P_spill = cos^(q+1) ψ₀.

The rim angle shrinks from 64.0° to about 34.7°, so cos ψ₀ grows and more of the same feed pattern spills past the rim. A shallower dish needs a narrower feed.

2. Why does the narrowest feed fail to maximize gain even though it spills almost nothing?

Consider how the aperture field varies from the centre to the edge.

Its power concentrates near the dish centre, so the outer aperture contributes little field and the dish behaves like a smaller one. Taper efficiency falls faster than spillover efficiency rises.
